question: TCS reports a Net Profit of ₹46,099 Cr on its Income Statement for FY24. Where does this number flow next, and how does it connect the three statements?
before: Net Profit is the critical link between all three statements. It flows two ways: (1) On the Balance Sheet, Net Profit (minus dividends paid) gets added to Retained Earnings within Shareholder Equity — this is how the company's accumulated profits build up over years. (2) On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Profit is the starting point of the Cash Flow from Operations section, after which non-cash items (like depreciation) and working capital changes are adjusted. Option A is wrong because Net Profit is an accounting measure, not cash — they are very different (accrual vs cash basis). Option C is wrong because last year's profit does not become next year's revenue. Option D is wrong because dividends are declared at management's discretion, not automatically owed. Mastering this linkage is the foundation of 3-statement modelling — coming up in Module 4.
after:
Concept: Net Profit is the earnings figure that bridges all three financial statements. It represents the company's bottom-line profitability calculated on an accrual basis.

Why this is correct: Net Profit flows to the Balance Sheet by increasing Retained Earnings (a component of Shareholder Equity) after accounting for dividends paid out. It also serves as the opening figure in the Cash Flow Statement's Operating Activities section, where non-cash items and working capital changes are then adjusted to reconcile accounting profit to actual cash generation. This dual flow ensures internal consistency across the three statements.

Why the others are wrong:

A) Net Profit cannot be added directly to Cash on the Balance Sheet. Net Profit is an accrual-basis accounting measure, while Cash is a balance sheet asset that reflects actual money. The two differ because accrual earnings include non-cash items like depreciation and changes in receivables. The reconciliation between them happens on the Cash Flow Statement, not directly on the Balance Sheet.

C) Prior-year Net Profit does not become next year's Revenue. Revenue is earned independently each period from the sale of goods or services, while Net Profit is derived from that year's revenue after deducting all expenses. Revenue appears on the Income Statement as the top line, not as a carryover from prior profits.

D) Net Profit is not recorded as a liability owed to shareholders. While companies may declare dividends from profits, the full Net Profit is not an automatic obligation. Management decides how much to distribute (dividend) and how much to retain (Retained Earnings), so the profit remains within equity, not on the liability side of the Balance Sheet.

Intuition: Understanding that Net Profit flows through Retained Earnings on the Balance Sheet and initiates the Cash Flow Statement is essential for building integrated financial models. It shows why profitability (Income Statement) and liquidity (Cash Flow Statement) must be analyzed together — a company can be profitable on paper yet short of cash if working capital or capital expenditures are not managed properly.
